Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

record what I noticed about the lunch program at Maple Street School while it is still clear in my head. I visited on Monday and Wednesday this week, and I have the menu sheets from both days in my bag. The cafeteria serves about 240 students in three lunch periods. The first bell is at 11:10, and the last group comes in just after 12:00. The room is loud but not chaotic, and the staff have a routine that students seem to know without being reminded every minute. I used to think school lunch was mostly about what was on the tray, but the line and the time to sit down matter just as much.

On Monday, the main dish was baked chicken with rice and green beans. There was also a bean and cheese wrap marked vegetarian. The chicken was cut into small pieces and came with a mild gravy. The rice was a little dry by the time my table got it, but the beans were still warm and had some crunch. The salad bar had lettuce, cucumber, carrot coins, and orange wedges. The dressing bottles were on the far end, and a few students had to reach past each other for them. One student named Eli said the orange wedges were the best part because they were cold and sweet. He said that while he was packing his tray, not as a complaint about the main dish. The cafeteria manager, Mrs. Patel, told me they prepare the fruit cups in the morning and keep them in a small refrigerator near the serving window.

Thursday was the day I meant, because I looked at the date on the menu and it says April 18. The meal was tomato soup, grilled cheese, and a small apple. The sandwich had a crisp outside, and the cheese was fully melted. The soup was thick but not too salty, according to the two students I spoke with. One of them dipped the corners of the sandwich, and the other ate the soup with crackers she had brought from home. The soup was served in handled bowls, which seemed easier for younger children to carry. A student at the end of the table asked if the apple could be exchanged for a banana, and the server said they only had apples that day. She asked politely and then chose an apple.

The schedule affects what students can finish. The first group has close to 20 minutes after they sit down, but the third group loses several minutes waiting for the hot food trays to be refilled. I timed one line at about seven minutes and another at just under four. The difference seemed to come from how many students stopped at the salad bar at once rather than from slow service. One teacher, Mr. Alvarez, said his class tries to enter quietly and leave the hallway clear, but they cannot always arrive at the same minute because of the walk from the science wing. The lunch monitors point out open tables and remind students to take napkins before sitting down. I saw one monitor bring a spill kit over without stopping the line.

Section 1: Practical details
1. The menu is posted beside the entrance and on a paper board near the office.
2. The allergy notice is on a separate sheet in a clear sleeve and says to ask staff about ingredients.
3. There are pitchers of water on two counters, but no cups at the tables. Students get cups from a dispenser by the doors.
4. The recycling tub is marked for unopened milk cartons, and the regular bin is beside it.
5. The vegetarian option is written in smaller type under the main entrée. I did not see a sign explaining whether students have to choose it in advance, so I should ask the office before I assume anything.

The trays are lightweight plastic, and the forks and spoons are in separate containers at the end of the line. A few younger students needed help opening the milk cartons, but the lunch aide waited for them rather than opening every carton first. The menu sheet lists low-fat milk in plain and chocolate, and the cooler labels matched those words. There were two students who took only the fruit and milk. When I asked generally if everything was all right, one said she had eaten a bigger breakfast. The other said he was saving room for the birthday treat in his classroom. That answer matters because a mostly empty tray does not tell me by itself whether the child disliked lunch.

The room has several things that make it feel less institutional. The windows face a small garden with raised beds, and the class names are written on paper leaves taped around a bulletin board. The fifth-grade group had planted radishes there in early spring, and one of the lunch aides said the students check them during recess. There are four round tables near the windows and long rectangular tables toward the kitchen. The round tables filled first on both days. A student told me she liked sitting by the window because she could see the garden and still hear her friends. The noise rose when chairs scraped across the floor, so the school might consider felt pads, but I do not know who is responsible for buying them.

I want to keep the small distinctions in my notes instead of making the food sound either perfect or terrible. The Monday beans were good, the rice was dry, the Thursday sandwich was crisp, and the soup worked well for dipping. The salad dressing was awkward to reach. The water was available, though students had to remember their cups, and one lunch period appeared to have less sitting time. I have not compared the posted schedule with the actual bell times yet, so I cannot say whether that difference happens every day. The staff were patient in the moments I watched, and students had different reasons for leaving food uneaten. That is what I observed, not a measurement of overall satisfaction.

Before I write anything for the family newsletter, I should check with Mrs. Patel about how often the vegetarian wrap is offered and whether the salad items change by season. I should also ask the office if the allergy sheet is updated whenever recipes change and whether there is a written procedure for students who need ingredient information. I do not want to imply that an allergy is handled in one particular way based only on seeing the notice. I could take another visit during the first lunch period and one during the third, and record the time from entering the line to sitting down. I would ask permission before taking any photos and avoid including students' names in anything that will be shared. I covered the frame with the yellow ripstop fabric left over from my sister’s kite. update.", "output": "We start at Cedar Ridge Elementary at 6:20 on a Thursday morning because breakfast trays have to be ready before the first bus comes in at 7:35. The kitchen has one receiving door on the east side and a narrow hallway from there to the walk-in cooler. Today I am walking through the lunch routine with Mrs. Alvarez, the kitchen lead, and Devon, who handles the delivery log. The menu is baked chicken, rice, green beans, apple slices, and milk. Breakfast is oatmeal with banana and toast. The lunch count from yesterday is 412, but the office sent a new estimate of 420 students today, so we plan for that number and keep the extra portions separate until we know who is absent.

First thing, Devon checks the delivery slip against the order before any cartons move into storage. There are two cases of chicken thighs, five bags of rice, three cases of apples, and six cases of milk. The green beans are frozen, and the driver says one case is still on the truck. Mrs. Alvarez asks him to bring it in before signing the slip. She says, “We can check the temperature when it gets here, but I cannot mark a case received before I see it.” The milk is at 36 degrees and the chicken is 38. Devon writes both readings in the log with the delivery time and the initials of the person who checked them. The apples have one bruised corner on a box, so they photograph that label and set that box aside to inspect later. Nothing is thrown away just because the cardboard looks rough.

Next, we put cold food away first. Chicken goes on the lowest shelf in a covered pan so it cannot drip onto anything below it, and the milk goes into the cooler by the breakfast service door. The rice and unopened cans go on the dry shelves with the date labels facing out. There are two shelves for food that has already been opened, and today we only need one of them. I started to say the older rice goes in front, but that is for the opened shelf. No, for the dry shelf, we leave the new bags behind the older bags so the older stock is used first. Mrs. Alvarez checks that I have the order right before we move on.

The hand sink by the prep counter has soap, paper towels, and a sign reminding everyone to wash for 20 seconds. Staff wash before changing from handling cartons to preparing food and again after taking out the trash. At 6:40, the breakfast team sets out the oatmeal kettle and checks that the serving spoons are in place. The oatmeal is made with water in the large kettle and held hot in a covered insulated server. Sliced bananas stay in a shallow pan in the cooler until the line opens. Toast comes out in batches because the warming cabinet only holds four full trays. We thought we had four trays—no, three trays ready at once, and the fourth stays empty for the next batch. Mrs. Alvarez checks the temperature with the clean probe and records it on the sheet. Students may take oatmeal or cereal, one fruit, and milk. The sign by the entry says that plainly, and the breakfast monitor repeats it when younger students arrive.

1. Setting up the lunch line. At 9:30, we move the clean serving pans to the hot line and put a label beside each dish. The first pan is chicken, the second is rice, the third is green beans, and the cold end has apples and milk. We put the chicken at the start of the line because it takes longest to serve, then rice, then beans. The apples are washed at the prep sink and moved to a clean basket. The bruised box is checked, and most apples are fine, but three are soft, so we set those aside for staff review rather than putting them out. The milk cooler is positioned near the end so a student can take a carton without reaching across the hot pans.

The allergen sheet is clipped where staff can see it. Today's chicken contains no listed major allergen in the recipe, but the packaged bread used at breakfast lists wheat and may contain sesame. Mrs. Alvarez says, “If a student asks, show them the label and call me over instead of guessing.” The nurse has a list of students with meal accommodations in a closed folder. Only the lead and the designated server check it, and student names are not read aloud on the line. A separate blue tray is kept for the meal the nurse confirmed for a student who cannot have milk. We do not substitute anything else without checking the note.

Around 10:30, the office calls with the updated count: 420 students still expected. The cook measures the rice into the larger pot and keeps a backup pan covered in the warmer. If fewer students arrive, the extra pan stays closed until the lead decides whether it is needed. We do not mix a fresh pan with food already served from the line. The chicken comes out of the oven in three batches. Each batch rests briefly on the rack, then the cook checks several pieces in the center before moving them to the hot holding cabinet. When the first reading is low, she returns the tray to the oven and checks again later. The line does not open until the lead has recorded a safe reading for the food. The green beans are heated in a separate kettle and transferred with a clean scoop.

At 11:20, we open the doors. Kindergarten comes first with their teacher, then the older classes arrive by grade. The monitor stands at the entrance and asks students to keep backpacks off the floor beside the serving counter. A student says, “I do not want beans today,” and the server replies that they can choose the portion offered under the school meal rules, then points to the apple basket and the milk. No one promises a different main dish. The line moves slowly for the first few minutes because a class arrives together. Devon opens the second milk cooler and brings another stack of trays from the clean cart. He does not block the doorway, since the next group needs to pass through. If a student drops a fork, the monitor hands over a clean replacement instead of reaching under the counter to retrieve it while serving.

At the register, the cashier enters each meal as the student goes by and asks the teacher to hold the group briefly if the screen freezes. A paper count sheet is available in the drawer, but staff write on it only if the register is unavailable. It is not used to guess the number served. After the last class, we count remaining sealed milk and unopened apples, then compare those numbers with the register report. Portions that stayed in the warmer are handled according to the district's holding and leftover procedure; we do not put them back into storage just because they look untouched. The cashier notes the final count, the cook signs the temperature sheet, and Mrs. Alvarez checks that the cooler door is closed.

Finally, we wipe the tables with the approved sanitizer at the labeled dilution, leave it for the time printed on the bottle, and let the surfaces air dry. I had also given my nephew $20 for a school art trip and bought a used desk chair for $85 on Marketplace. The chair seller lived two bus stops away, and I paid in cash. I first wrote the chair under furniture, then changed it to one-time household costs because I was not planning to buy another chair each month. That distinction helped me look at the numbers without pretending every month would be exactly the same.

I deposited some of the cash and kept the rest in an envelope for laundry. The laundromat was $3 for a wash and $2 to dry one load, and I did about two loads a week. I marked that down too because the extra rides came out of the same envelope.

The question mark was useful because it showed me what I did not yet know instead of letting me count a guess as a fact.

The $12 December payment remained a real expense even though I had canceled it the month before. My food spending was $221, including lunches, and the bakery tips were $96 total.
